A diffusion or flow model generates by solving an ordinary differential equation: tens of network calls per sample. This post is about doing it with one. Below is the series' toy again, a ring of eight Gaussians, with 500 noise points and the exact flow that carries them onto the ring. Drag the slider to choose how far to jump; click anywhere to pick the highlighted point:

<figure class="fig" data-chord>

*What to try.* With the slider at $r = 0$, the flow map puts 99% of the points on a mode. Switch to one Euler step: every point lands on the centre of the ring, and none is on a mode. For the highlighted point, the dashed arrow is the tangent to its path at the start, which is what a velocity field gives you. The solid arrow is the chord from start to end, which is what a one-step generator needs. Slide $r$ toward 1 and the chord shortens and turns into the tangent. Every method in this post is a way of learning the solid arrow.

This is the last post of the series on deep generative models, after [the map](/aboutme/blog/generative-models-one-map/), [diffusion models](/aboutme/blog/diffusion-models-from-first-principles/) and [flow matching](/aboutme/blog/flow-matching/). Both of the last two ended at the same wall: one step from pure noise returns the mean of the data. This post answers five questions:

1. **Why does one step fail even with a perfect velocity field, and what should be learned instead?** (Sections 1 and 2.)
2. **Which equations pin that object down, so it can be learned without solving the ODE?** (Section 3.)
3. **How do consistency models, shortcut models and MeanFlow follow from those equations?** (Sections 4 to 6.)
4. **How do methods that skip trajectories and match the distribution directly work, from DMD to drifting models?** (Sections 7 and 8.)
5. **How do they compare on one toy, and which to use when?** (Sections 9 to 11.)

Every result has a folded proof in numbered steps. The toy's velocity has a closed form, so the exact flow map sits next to seven trained one-step models.

## Notation

Data at $t = 0$, noise at $t = 1$, linear path, as in the flow-matching post. Some papers cited here use the opposite convention; their formulas are flipped. The flow-matching post wrote $\boldsymbol{u}$ for one pair's velocity; here that is written out as $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{x}_0$, and $\boldsymbol{u}$ means the average velocity.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\boldsymbol{x}_t = (1 - t)\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ | the path; $\boldsymbol{x}_0 \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}$, $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ independent |
| $\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}, t) = \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{x}_0 \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t = \boldsymbol{x}]$ | the marginal velocity; $p_t$ is the law of $\boldsymbol{x}_t$ |
| $\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})$ | the flow map: where the ODE $\dot{\boldsymbol{x}} = \boldsymbol{v}$ started at $\boldsymbol{x}$ at time $t$ is at time $r$ |
| $\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, r, t) = \dfrac{\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})}{t - r}$ | the average velocity over $[r, t]$ |
| $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}, t) = \boldsymbol{X}_{t\to 0}(\boldsymbol{x})$ | the consistency function: jump straight to data |
| $\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{F}$ | the Jacobian matrix of a map $\boldsymbol{F}$; $(\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{F})\boldsymbol{w}$ is a Jacobian–vector product |
| $\operatorname{sg}[\cdot]$ | stop-gradient: the value is used, but no gradient flows through it |
| $\boldsymbol{G}_\theta$, $q_\theta$ | a one-step generator and the law of $\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})$ |

Throughout, $\boldsymbol{v}$ is assumed smooth enough for the ODE to have unique solutions. For the toy this holds at every $t > 0$.

## 1. Why one step fails

The flow-matching post proved that for the linear path a single Euler step from noise gives $\boldsymbol{x}_1 - \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_1, 1) = \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{x}_0]$, whatever $\boldsymbol{x}_1$ is. The figure's Euler mode shows it: all 500 points land on the centre. Nothing in this is a modelling error. The figure uses the exact velocity.

What fails is the object. Euler's method assumes the velocity stays what it was at the start. Writing the true jump as an integral of the velocity along the path, its error is

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}) - \big(\boldsymbol{x} - (t - r)\,\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}, t)\big) \\
&\qquad = -\int_r^t \big(\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_s, s) - \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}, t)\big)\,ds,
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{x}_s = \boldsymbol{X}_{t\to s}(\boldsymbol{x})$ is the path. It is zero only if the velocity is constant along the path, that is, if paths are straight lines run at constant speed. The flow-matching post straightened paths by pairing points with optimal transport and by reflow. That took one step from 0% to 76% and 88% of samples on a mode, and no further: a finite network never makes every path exactly straight.

The other way is to stop asking for the velocity. A velocity field answers "which way now?". A one-step generator needs the answer to "where do I end up?", and that question has its own object.

## 2. The flow map

:::definition[Flow map]
For $r, t \in [0, 1]$, $\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})$ is the value at time $r$ of the solution of $\dot{\boldsymbol{x}} = \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}, s)$ that passes through $\boldsymbol{x}$ at time $t$.
:::

It is defined in both directions of time, but generation only uses $r < t$, toward the data.

:::proposition[Properties of the flow map]
1. **Identity:** $\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to t}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{x}$.
2. **Semigroup:** $\boldsymbol{X}_{s\to r}\big(\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to s}(\boldsymbol{x})\big) = \boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})$ for all $t, s, r$.
3. **Lagrangian equation:** $\partial_r\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{v}\big(\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}), r\big)$.
4. **Eulerian equation:** $\partial_t\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}) + \big(\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})\big)\,\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}, t) = \mathbf{0}$.
5. **Transport:** if $\boldsymbol{x} \sim p_t$ then $\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}) \sim p_r$. In particular $\boldsymbol{X}_{1\to 0}$ maps $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ exactly onto $p_{\mathrm{data}}$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Identity and Lagrangian equation.** Both are the definition: the solution passes through $\boldsymbol{x}$ at time $t$, and its time derivative is the velocity at its current position.

**Step 2. Semigroup.** Start at $\boldsymbol{x}$ at time $t$ and follow the ODE to time $s$, reaching $\boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X}_{t\to s}(\boldsymbol{x})$. The solution through $\boldsymbol{y}$ at time $s$ and the original solution agree at time $s$, so by uniqueness they are the same curve. Its value at $r$ is $\boldsymbol{X}_{s\to r}(\boldsymbol{y})$ on one side and $\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})$ on the other.

**Step 3. The end point does not depend on where you start along a path.** Let $\boldsymbol{x}_s$, $s \in [0, 1]$, be one solution of the ODE. By Step 2, $\boldsymbol{X}_{s\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}_s) = \boldsymbol{x}_r$ for every $s$, so $g(s) = \boldsymbol{X}_{s\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}_s)$ is constant.

**Step 4. Differentiate.** By the chain rule, $g'(s) = \partial_s\boldsymbol{X}_{s\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}_s) + \big(\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{X}_{s\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}_s)\big)\,\dot{\boldsymbol{x}}_s$, with $\dot{\boldsymbol{x}}_s = \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_s, s)$. Since $g$ is constant, this is zero. Every point lies on some solution, so the Eulerian equation holds at every $(\boldsymbol{x}, t)$.

**Step 5. Transport.** The flow-matching post showed that the marginal velocity generates the path: if a point is drawn from $p_t$ and moved by the ODE, it is distributed as $p_r$ at time $r$. Moving it by the ODE is applying $\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}$. At $t = 1$, $p_1 = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$; at $r = 0$, $p_0 = p_{\mathrm{data}}$.
:::

Property 5 is the point: **a one-step generator that is perfect exists.** It is $\boldsymbol{X}_{1\to 0}$, and it is a deterministic function of the noise. On the toy, applying the exact map to 4000 noise points puts 99% of them on a mode, all eight modes covered.

It helps to factor out the trivial part of the jump. Define the **average velocity** over $[r, t]$ by $\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{x} - (t - r)\,\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, r, t)$. Along a path, by the Lagrangian equation,

$$
\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, r, t) = \frac{\boldsymbol{x}_t - \boldsymbol{x}_r}{t - r} = \frac{1}{t - r}\int_r^t \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_s, s)\,ds,
$$

which is the slope of the chord in the figure. As $r \to t$ the average becomes the instantaneous value, $\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, t, t) = \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}, t)$. This is why many methods below can train the diagonal $r = t$ with ordinary flow matching. One step is then $\boldsymbol{x}_0 = \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}, 0, 1)$. The figure's readout gives $|\boldsymbol{u}|$, $|\boldsymbol{v}|$ and the angle between them for the chosen point. For points near the centre the angle is large, because their paths start toward the mean and only later turn toward a mode.

The animation below shows the same objects in one dimension: the tangent, the chord, the average velocity as $r$ moves, and the consistency property used in Section 4.

<figure class="fig">
<video src="/aboutme/blog/one-step/flowmap.mp4" autoplay muted loop playsinline controls poster="/aboutme/blog/one-step/flowmap.jpg"></video>
<figcaption>Space-time picture in one dimension (data at ±1 on the right, noise on the left). A velocity field gives each path's tangent: one long step along it lands on the mean. A flow map gives the chord from start to end. The average velocity is the slope of the chord down to time r, and becomes the tangent as r approaches t. Consistency: from anywhere on a path, the jump to t = 0 lands on the same point.</figcaption>

### Why not regress on the map directly?

You can. Draw noise $\boldsymbol{z}$, solve the ODE with a trained teacher to get $\boldsymbol{X}_{1\to 0}(\boldsymbol{z})$, and fit a network to the pairs by least squares (Luhman and Luhman, 2021). On the toy, with 100,000 pairs from the exact ODE, the distilled map puts 98% of samples on a mode, as good as the exact map. The cost is the pairs. Each one needs a full ODE solve with the teacher (here 100 Runge–Kutta steps, 400 velocity evaluations), and on images the fixed set of pairs is a bottleneck. Every method below replaces the full solve with something local: a property of the map that one or two extra network calls can check.

Here is the whole landscape before going through it. The left column learns the flow map, sorted by which property of the map the loss enforces. The right column skips trajectories and matches the output distribution.

## 3. Three equations that pin the map down

Properties 2 to 4 are not just true of the flow map. Each one, together with the identity and the velocity on the diagonal, determines it.

:::theorem[Characterisations of the flow map (Boffi, Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2025)]
Let $\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r}$ be a family of smooth maps with $\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to t} = \mathrm{id}$. Each of the following implies $\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r} = \boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}$ for all $t, r$:

(a) **Lagrangian:** $\partial_r\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{v}\big(\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}), r\big)$.

(b) **Eulerian:** $\partial_t\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}) + \big(\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})\big)\,\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}, t) = \mathbf{0}$.

(c) **Semigroup plus tangent:** $\boldsymbol{Y}_{s\to r}\circ\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to s} = \boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r}$, and $\partial_r\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})\big|_{r = t} = \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}, t)$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. (a).** Fix $t$ and $\boldsymbol{x}$. Both $r \mapsto \boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})$ and $r \mapsto \boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})$ solve $\dot{\boldsymbol{y}} = \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{y}, r)$ with the value $\boldsymbol{x}$ at $r = t$. Solutions are unique, so they coincide.

**Step 2. (b).** Let $\boldsymbol{x}_s$ be a true path through $\boldsymbol{x}$ at time $t$, and $g(s) = \boldsymbol{Y}_{s\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}_s)$. By the chain rule and (b), $g'(s) = \partial_s\boldsymbol{Y}_{s\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}_s) + (\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{Y}_{s\to r})\,\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_s, s) = \mathbf{0}$, so $g$ is constant. Then $g(t) = g(r)$, and $g(r) = \boldsymbol{Y}_{r\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}_r) = \boldsymbol{x}_r$ by the identity. So $\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{x}_r = \boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})$.

**Step 3. (c) implies (a).** By the semigroup property, $\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r+h}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{Y}_{r\to r+h}(\boldsymbol{y})$ with $\boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})$. Differentiate in $h$ at $h = 0$. The left side gives $\partial_r\boldsymbol{Y}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x})$. The right side gives the tangent condition at $(\boldsymbol{y}, r)$, namely $\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{y}, r)$. That is (a), and Step 1 finishes.
:::

The theorem turns a hard target, the end point of an ODE solve, into local checks, each costing one or two network calls. Every method in the next three sections has the same two parts: **the diagonal**, taught by flow matching or by a teacher's velocity, and **one off-diagonal property**, enforced with a target the model computes from itself under a stop-gradient. Boffi et al. call this self-distillation.

| property | what the loss compares | methods |
|---|---|---|
| semigroup (c) | one long jump against two shorter ones | progressive distillation, consistency models, consistency trajectory models, shortcut models |
| Eulerian (b) | the jump's end, as its start slides along a path | continuous-time consistency models (sCM), MeanFlow, α-Flow |
| Lagrangian (a) | the jump's end moving with the velocity field | Lagrangian self-distillation (Boffi et al., 2025) |

Progressive distillation (Salimans and Ho, 2022) is the simplest semigroup method. It trains a student to match two teacher steps with one, then makes the student the teacher and repeats, halving the step count each round. The rest of the table needs more explanation.

## 4. Consistency models

A **consistency model** (Song, Dhariwal, Chen and Sutskever, 2023) learns only the slice $r = 0$: the consistency function $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}, t) = \boldsymbol{X}_{t\to 0}(\boldsymbol{x})$. Its defining property is Step 3 of the first proof with $r = 0$: along any path, $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) = \boldsymbol{x}_0$ for every $t$. The identity is built into the parametrisation, $\boldsymbol{f}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}, t) = c_{\mathrm{skip}}(t)\,\boldsymbol{x} + c_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\,\boldsymbol{F}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}, t)$ with $c_{\mathrm{skip}}(0) = 1$ and $c_{\mathrm{out}}(0) = 0$. For the linear path the natural choice is $\boldsymbol{f}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}, t) = \boldsymbol{x} - t\,\boldsymbol{F}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}, t)$. Then $\boldsymbol{F}_\theta$ estimates the average velocity $\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, 0, t)$: a consistency model is a MeanFlow network restricted to $r = 0$.

**Consistency distillation (CD).** Cut $[0, 1]$ into a grid $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_N = 1$ with spacing $\Delta$. Draw a point $\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{n+1}}$ on the path, take one step of an ODE solver with a teacher's velocity to get $\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{t_n} = \boldsymbol{x}_{t_{n+1}} - \Delta\,\boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{teacher}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{n+1}}, t_{n+1})$, and minimise

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CD}} = \mathbb{E}\,\big\lVert \boldsymbol{f}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_{t_{n+1}}, t_{n+1}) - \operatorname{sg}\big[\boldsymbol{f}_\theta(\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{t_n}, t_n)\big] \big\rVert^2 .
$$

The original paper used an exponential moving average of $\theta$ inside the stop-gradient; later work uses $\theta$ itself. This is the semigroup property on adjacent grid times: one solver step followed by a jump to data should equal a jump to data.

:::proposition[A zero CD loss recovers the solver's map]
Let $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_n(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{x} - \Delta\,\boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{teacher}}(\boldsymbol{x}, t_{n+1})$ be the solver step from $t_{n+1}$ to $t_n$. If $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}, t_0) = \boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}, t_{n+1}) = \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\Phi}_n(\boldsymbol{x}), t_n)$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}$ and $n$, then $\boldsymbol{f}(\cdot, t_n) = \boldsymbol{\Phi}_0\circ\boldsymbol{\Phi}_1\circ\dots\circ\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{n-1}$. In particular $\boldsymbol{f}(\cdot, 1)$ is the $N$-step solver's map from noise to data.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. $n = 1$:** $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}, t_1) = \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\Phi}_0(\boldsymbol{x}), t_0) = \boldsymbol{\Phi}_0(\boldsymbol{x})$, using the boundary condition.

**Step 2. Induction:** if $\boldsymbol{f}(\cdot, t_n) = \boldsymbol{\Phi}_0\circ\dots\circ\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{n-1}$, then $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}, t_{n+1}) = \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\Phi}_n(\boldsymbol{x}), t_n) = \boldsymbol{\Phi}_0\circ\dots\circ\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{n-1}(\boldsymbol{\Phi}_n(\boldsymbol{x}))$.

**Step 3. Error.** The $N$-step solution differs from the exact flow map by the solver's global error: $O(\Delta)$ for Euler, $O(\Delta^p)$ for a solver of order $p$. Song et al. (2023) state this bound, and use the second-order Heun solver.
:::

The proof also shows a weakness. The only anchor is the boundary $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}, 0) = \boldsymbol{x}$. The target at $t_n$ is right only once $\boldsymbol{f}$ is right at $t_{n-1}$, so correct information moves up the grid one cell at a time. On the toy, CD with a fixed grid of 160 cells from the first step learned almost nothing in 30,000 steps: 6% of one-step samples on a mode. With the grid coarse at first (10 cells) and doubled every 5,000 steps up to 320, the same CD puts 89% on a mode. Coarse-to-fine schedules of this kind are standard (Song and Dhariwal, 2024).

**Consistency training (CT)** removes the teacher. The teacher's velocity is replaced by the velocity of the training pair itself, $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{x}_0$. Then $\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{t_n} = \boldsymbol{x}_{t_{n+1}} - \Delta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{x}_0) = (1 - t_n)\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t_n\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$: the same pair, at the earlier time. This is the trick of conditional flow matching again, and it is unbiased for the same reason.

:::proposition[CT matches CD to first order (Song et al., 2023)]
Let $\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{x}_{t_{n+1}}$, $\boldsymbol{w} = \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{x}_0$ and $\boldsymbol{v} = \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{w} \mid \boldsymbol{x}]$. The gradient of the CT loss equals the gradient of the CD loss with the exact teacher $\boldsymbol{v}$, up to a term of order $\Delta^2$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. The gradient.** For a target $\boldsymbol{y}$ under a stop-gradient, $\nabla_\theta\,\mathbb{E}\lVert\boldsymbol{f}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}, t_{n+1}) - \operatorname{sg}[\boldsymbol{y}]\rVert^2 = 2\,\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{J}_\theta^\top(\boldsymbol{f}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}, t_{n+1}) - \boldsymbol{y})\big]$, with $\mathbf{J}_\theta = \partial_\theta\boldsymbol{f}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}, t_{n+1})$. The two losses differ only in $\boldsymbol{y}$.

**Step 2. Expand the CT target.** Taylor-expand $\boldsymbol{f}(\cdot, t_n)$ around $\boldsymbol{x} - \Delta\boldsymbol{v}$:
$\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x} - \Delta\boldsymbol{w}, t_n) = \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x} - \Delta\boldsymbol{v}, t_n) - \Delta\,\mathbf{A}\,(\boldsymbol{w} - \boldsymbol{v}) + O(\Delta^2)$,
where $\mathbf{A} = \partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x} - \Delta\boldsymbol{v}, t_n)$ depends on $\boldsymbol{x}$ only.

**Step 3. Take the difference of gradients.** CT minus CD is $2\Delta\,\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{J}_\theta^\top\mathbf{A}\,(\boldsymbol{w} - \boldsymbol{v})\big] + O(\Delta^2)$.

**Step 4. Condition on $\boldsymbol{x}$.** $\mathbf{J}_\theta$ and $\mathbf{A}$ are functions of $\boldsymbol{x}$, and $\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{w} - \boldsymbol{v} \mid \boldsymbol{x}] = \mathbf{0}$. By the tower rule the first term is zero. What remains is $O(\Delta^2)$, and it contains the variance of $\boldsymbol{w}$ given $\boldsymbol{x}$: the extra noise CT pays for having no teacher.
:::

On the toy, with the same schedule and budget, CT puts 68% of one-step samples on a mode against 89% for CD with the exact teacher. The gap is the $O(\Delta^2)$ noise term of the proof. Improved consistency training (iCT; Song and Dhariwal, 2024) closed much of it on images. It drops the moving average, uses a pseudo-Huber loss, a log-normal schedule over noise levels and the doubling grid, and reports one-step FID 2.51 on CIFAR-10 and 3.25 on ImageNet 64×64. Easy consistency tuning (ECT; Geng, Pokle, Luo, Lin and Kolter, 2024) starts from a pretrained diffusion model and shrinks $\Delta$ gradually, reaching two-step FID 2.73 on CIFAR-10 in about an hour on one GPU.

**Sampling in several steps.** A consistency model only knows jumps to $t = 0$, so to take more steps it re-noises: jump to data, $\boldsymbol{x} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}, 1)$; push the result back to an intermediate time with fresh noise, $\boldsymbol{x}_s = (1 - s)\boldsymbol{x} + s\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}'$; jump again, $\boldsymbol{x} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_s, s)$. If $\boldsymbol{f}$ were exact, $\boldsymbol{x}$ would be a data sample, so $\boldsymbol{x}_s \sim p_s$, which is what $\boldsymbol{f}(\cdot, s)$ expects. With an imperfect $\boldsymbol{f}$, the fresh noise washes out part of the error.

**The continuous-time limit.** Let $\Delta \to 0$ with the stop-gradient copy equal to $\theta$. A first-order expansion gives
$\boldsymbol{f}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) - \boldsymbol{f}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_t - \Delta\boldsymbol{v}, t - \Delta) = \Delta\,\tfrac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{f}_\theta + O(\Delta^2)$, with $\tfrac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{f}_\theta = \partial_t\boldsymbol{f}_\theta + (\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{f}_\theta)\,\boldsymbol{v}$. So the CD gradient, divided by $\Delta$, tends to $2\,\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{J}_\theta^\top\operatorname{sg}[\tfrac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{f}_\theta]\big]$. Training drives $\tfrac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{f}_\theta$ to zero along paths. That is the Eulerian equation (b) with $r = 0$, and the total derivative is one Jacobian–vector product. Continuous-time consistency models (sCM; Lu and Song, 2025) make this stable at scale, with a new parametrisation of the path and normalisation of the tangent. They report two-step FID 1.88 on ImageNet 512×512 with 1.5 billion parameters. Consistency trajectory models (CTM; Kim et al., 2024) go the other way and learn the full two-time map $\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}$.

## 5. Shortcut models

A **shortcut model** (Frans, Hafner, Levine and Abbeel, 2025) learns the average velocity for a given step size: $\boldsymbol{s}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}, t, d) \approx \boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, t - d, t)$, so that $\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to t-d}(\boldsymbol{x}) \approx \boldsymbol{x} - d\,\boldsymbol{s}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}, t, d)$. The paper puts noise at $t = 0$; here it is flipped. The rule that trains it is the semigroup property written for average velocities.

:::proposition[Doubling rule]
With $\boldsymbol{x}' = \boldsymbol{x} - d\,\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, t - d, t)$, the exact average velocity satisfies
$$
\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, t - 2d, t) = \tfrac{1}{2}\big[\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, t - d, t) + \boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}', t - 2d, t - d)\big].
$$
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Split the jump.** By the semigroup property, $\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to t-2d}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{X}_{t-d\to t-2d}(\boldsymbol{x}')$ with $\boldsymbol{x}' = \boldsymbol{X}_{t\to t-d}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{x} - d\,\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, t - d, t)$.

**Step 2. Write each jump with its average velocity.** The left side is $\boldsymbol{x} - 2d\,\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, t - 2d, t)$. The right side is $\boldsymbol{x}' - d\,\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}', t - 2d, t - d) = \boldsymbol{x} - d\,\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, t - d, t) - d\,\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}', t - 2d, t - d)$.

**Step 3.** Equate, cancel $\boldsymbol{x}$, and divide by $-2d$.
:::

Training mixes two losses. For $d = 0$, the shortcut is the instantaneous velocity, and it is trained by flow matching on $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{x}_0$. For $d \in \{\tfrac{1}{128}, \tfrac{1}{64}, \dots, 1\}$ the target is the right side of the doubling rule, computed by the network with half the step under a stop-gradient. The paper gives a quarter of each batch to this bootstrap term. Each level is trained from the one below, and the bottom level from flow matching. At sampling time, choose $N$ steps and use $d = 1/N$: one model gives every step count from 1 to 128.

On the toy, the shortcut model puts 89% of one-step samples on a mode, rising to 95% with 4 steps and 98% with 8.

## 6. MeanFlow

**MeanFlow** (Geng, Deng, Bai, Kolter and He, 2025) learns the average velocity $\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, r, t)$ for every pair $r \le t$. It trains with an identity that follows from the definition. The time convention matches this series: noise at $t = 1$, and one step is $\boldsymbol{x}_0 = \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{u}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}, 0, 1)$.

:::theorem[The MeanFlow identity]
Along any path $\boldsymbol{x}_t$ of the ODE, for fixed $r$,
$$
\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, r, t) = \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) - (t - r)\,\frac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, r, t),
$$

where

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{u} = \big(\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{u}\big)\,\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) + \partial_t\boldsymbol{u}.
$$
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Multiply out the definition.** $(t - r)\,\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, r, t) = \int_r^t\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_s, s)\,ds$.

**Step 2. Differentiate both sides in $t$, with $r$ fixed and $\boldsymbol{x}_t$ moving along the path.** The left side gives $\boldsymbol{u} + (t - r)\,\frac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{u}$ by the product rule. The right side gives $\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus.

**Step 3.** Equate and rearrange to get the identity.

**Step 4. The total derivative.** $\boldsymbol{u}$ depends on $t$ through its first argument, which moves at $\dot{\boldsymbol{x}}_t = \boldsymbol{v}$, and through its third. The second argument $r$ is fixed. The chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{u} = (\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{u})\boldsymbol{v} + 0\cdot\partial_r\boldsymbol{u} + 1\cdot\partial_t\boldsymbol{u}$: the Jacobian–vector product of $\boldsymbol{u}$ with the tangent $(\boldsymbol{v}, 0, 1)$ in $(\boldsymbol{x}, r, t)$.
:::

The identity is the Eulerian equation in average-velocity form. Substitute $\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}_t) = \boldsymbol{x}_t - (t - r)\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, r, t)$ into "the end point does not move along a path": $\frac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{X}_{t\to r}(\boldsymbol{x}_t) = \boldsymbol{v} - \boldsymbol{u} - (t - r)\frac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{u} = \mathbf{0}$, which is the same equation. Boffi et al. (2025) make this observation. The identity also pins $\boldsymbol{u}$ down completely.

:::proposition[The identity determines the average velocity]
If a bounded function $\tilde{\boldsymbol{u}}$ satisfies the MeanFlow identity along every path and for every $r \le t$, then $\tilde{\boldsymbol{u}} = \boldsymbol{u}$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1.** Fix a path and $r$, and let $\boldsymbol{g}(t) = (t - r)\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{u}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, r, t) - \int_r^t\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_s, s)\,ds$.

**Step 2.** $\boldsymbol{g}(r) = \mathbf{0}$, because $\tilde{\boldsymbol{u}}$ is bounded and multiplied by $t - r = 0$.

**Step 3.** $\boldsymbol{g}'(t) = \tilde{\boldsymbol{u}} + (t - r)\frac{d}{dt}\tilde{\boldsymbol{u}} - \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t) = \mathbf{0}$ by the identity.

**Step 4.** So $\boldsymbol{g} \equiv \mathbf{0}$, and $\tilde{\boldsymbol{u}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, r, t) = \frac{1}{t - r}\int_r^t\boldsymbol{v}\,ds = \boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, r, t)$.
:::

**The training loss.** Turn the identity into a regression target with the network on both sides, and stop the gradient through the target:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}\,\big\lVert \boldsymbol{u}_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_t, r, t) - \operatorname{sg}[\boldsymbol{u}_{\mathrm{tgt}}] \big\rVert^2,
$$

$$
\boldsymbol{u}_{\mathrm{tgt}} = \boldsymbol{w} - (t - r)\big[(\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{u}_\theta)\,\boldsymbol{w} + \partial_t\boldsymbol{u}_\theta\big].
$$

The unknown marginal velocity has been replaced by the pair's velocity $\boldsymbol{w} = \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{x}_0$, in both places it appears. That is allowed for the usual reason.

:::proposition[The pair's velocity gives the right gradient]
For fixed $\theta$, the gradient of $\mathcal{L}$ is unchanged if $\boldsymbol{w}$ is replaced by $\boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. The target is affine in $\boldsymbol{w}$.** $\boldsymbol{u}_{\mathrm{tgt}} = \mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{w} + \boldsymbol{b}$, with $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{I} - (t - r)\,\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{u}_\theta$ and $\boldsymbol{b} = -(t - r)\,\partial_t\boldsymbol{u}_\theta$. Both are evaluated at $(\boldsymbol{x}_t, r, t)$, and a Jacobian–vector product is linear in its vector.

**Step 2. The gradient is linear in the target.** $\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L} = 2\,\mathbb{E}\big[(\partial_\theta\boldsymbol{u}_\theta)^\top(\boldsymbol{u}_\theta - \mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{w} - \boldsymbol{b})\big]$, and $\partial_\theta\boldsymbol{u}_\theta$, $\mathbf{M}$, $\boldsymbol{b}$ depend only on $(\boldsymbol{x}_t, r, t)$.

**Step 3. Condition.** $\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{w} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t] = \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{x}_t, t)$, so by the tower rule $\boldsymbol{w}$ can be replaced by $\boldsymbol{v}$ inside the expectation.
:::

Three implementation details matter. First, $(\partial_{\boldsymbol{x}}\boldsymbol{u}_\theta)\boldsymbol{w} + \partial_t\boldsymbol{u}_\theta$ is one forward-mode Jacobian–vector product, computed alongside $\boldsymbol{u}_\theta$ itself at roughly the cost of an extra forward pass. The stop-gradient means no second derivatives are needed. Second, a share of each batch uses $r = t$, where the loss reduces to flow matching. In the paper's ablation, using $r = t$ always (pure flow matching) gives one-step FID 328.91; making 25% of pairs have $r \ne t$ gives the best result, 61.06, in that small setting. Third, the paper weights each example by $1/(\lVert\text{error}\rVert^2 + c)^p$, with $p = 1$ by default.

On the toy, MeanFlow with these settings puts 98% of one-step samples on a mode, and 99.8% with 4 steps. That is more than the data itself: only 98.8% of data points lie within three standard deviations of a centre. It is a warning sign, not a success. The modes are too narrow, with a standard deviation of 0.04 to 0.06 against the data's 0.10. With several steps they are also pushed outward, by 0.09 to 0.11, about one standard deviation, and the energy distance to the data grows from 7 to 20 ($\times 10^{-3}$) as steps are added.

The last proposition shows how this can happen. Replacing $\boldsymbol{v}$ by the pair's velocity is unbiased for the squared error, because the gradient is linear in the target. The adaptive weight depends on the error, and so on $\boldsymbol{w}$, and Step 3 of the proof no longer goes through: the weight buys lower variance with bias. With plain squared error, MeanFlow puts 84%, 86% and 95% of samples on a mode with 1, 2 and 4 steps, and its modes stay centred (offsets within 0.01 beyond one step). On images the paper's ablation found that the weighting improves FID. The toy shows what it can cost. On ImageNet 256×256, trained from scratch with no distillation, the paper reports one-step FID 3.43, and 2.20 with two steps for its largest model.

Two follow-ups sharpen the picture. **α-Flow** (Zhang et al., 2026) shows that the MeanFlow loss splits into a trajectory flow-matching term and a trajectory-consistency term, whose gradients are strongly negatively correlated. It defines a family of objectives that contains flow matching, shortcut models and MeanFlow, and moves from one end to the other by a curriculum. It reports one-step FID 2.58. **Improved MeanFlow** (Geng, Lu, Wu, Shechtman, Kolter and He, 2026) rewrites the objective as a loss on the instantaneous velocity, reparametrised through the network for $\boldsymbol{u}$, and treats guidance as a conditioning input. It reports one-step FID 1.72.

## 7. Matching the distribution instead

Every method so far learns one particular map, the one the ODE defines. But a one-step generator needs only $q_\theta = p_{\mathrm{data}}$: any $\boldsymbol{G}_\theta$ that pushes the noise onto the data will do, and many do. The second family never mentions trajectories. It compares samples of $\boldsymbol{G}_\theta$ with the data and moves the samples.

### With a teacher's scores: distribution matching distillation

Take the reverse KL divergence $\mathrm{KL}(q_\theta\,\|\,p)$ as the objective. Its gradient needs only two score functions.

:::proposition[Gradient of the reverse KL]
With $\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})$,
$$
\nabla_\theta\,\mathrm{KL}(q_\theta\,\|\,p) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\Big[\big(\partial_\theta\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})\big)^\top\big(\nabla\log q_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}) - \nabla\log p(\boldsymbol{x})\big)\Big].
$$
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Write the divergence as an expectation over noise.** $\mathrm{KL}(q_\theta\,\|\,p) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\big[\log q_\theta(\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})) - \log p(\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}))\big]$.

**Step 2. Two routes for $\theta$.** The integrand depends on $\theta$ through the sample $\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})$, and through the subscript of $q_\theta$.

**Step 3. The subscript route vanishes.** $\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\big[\partial_\theta\log q_\theta(\boldsymbol{x})\big|_{\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})}\big] = \int q_\theta\,\partial_\theta\log q_\theta\,d\boldsymbol{x} = \partial_\theta\!\int q_\theta\,d\boldsymbol{x} = \partial_\theta 1 = 0$.

**Step 4. The sample route.** By the chain rule it is $(\partial_\theta\boldsymbol{G}_\theta)^\top\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}}\big(\log q_\theta - \log p\big)$.
:::

So gradient descent moves each output along $\nabla\log p - \nabla\log q_\theta$: toward where the data is denser, and away from where the generator already puts its samples. Clean-data scores are poorly defined off the data, so **DMD** (Yin et al., 2024) uses noised versions $p_t$ and $q_{\theta,t}$ at random $t$, as the series' opener argued for any divergence that needs overlapping supports. The score of $p_t$ comes from a pretrained diffusion model. The score of $q_{\theta,t}$ comes from a second diffusion model, trained online on the generator's outputs. Reverse KL is mode-seeking, so DMD adds a regression loss on teacher noise–image pairs. It reports one-step FID 2.62 on ImageNet 64×64. **DMD2** (Yin et al., 2024) removes the regression loss, updates the second diffusion model more often than the generator, and adds a GAN loss on real images. It reports 1.28 on the same benchmark, better than its teacher.

### With a discriminator, and with moments

A GAN is a one-step generator by construction; the opener derived its objective. **Adversarial diffusion distillation** (ADD; Sauer, Lorenz, Blattmann and Rombach, 2024) combines a GAN loss with score distillation from a pretrained diffusion model. It produced SDXL-Turbo, and its latent version (LADD; Sauer et al., 2024) made fast versions of larger text-to-image models.

**Inductive moment matching** (IMM; Zhou, Ermon and Song, 2025) sits between the two families. It learns jumps from time $t$ to any earlier time $s$, like a flow map. But its loss compares distributions, not points: the samples reached from $t$ against the samples the model itself reaches from a slightly earlier time $r$, measured by maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), the kernel distance from the opener. It is consistency, imposed in distribution. It is trained from scratch in one stage and reports FID 1.99 with 8 steps on ImageNet 256×256, and two-step FID 1.98 on CIFAR-10.

## 8. Drifting models

**Drifting models** (Deng, Li, Li, Du and He, 2026) move the iteration out of sampling and into training. The generator $\boldsymbol{G}_\theta$ is one network call. During training its output distribution $q_\theta$ is pushed toward $p_{\mathrm{data}}$ by a *drifting field*, a vector at every point that says where a sample there should move. The field is built from two kinds of samples: positives $\boldsymbol{y}^+ \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}$ and negatives $\boldsymbol{y}^- \sim q_\theta$. With the kernel $k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}) = \exp(-\lVert\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{y}\rVert/\tau)$,

$$
\boldsymbol{V}^+_p(\boldsymbol{x}) = \frac{\mathbb{E}_p\big[k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}^+)\,(\boldsymbol{y}^+ - \boldsymbol{x})\big]}{\mathbb{E}_p\big[k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}^+)\big]},
$$

$$
\boldsymbol{V}^-_q(\boldsymbol{x}) = \frac{\mathbb{E}_q\big[k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}^-)\,(\boldsymbol{y}^- - \boldsymbol{x})\big]}{\mathbb{E}_q\big[k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}^-)\big]},
$$

$$
\boldsymbol{V}_{p,q}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{V}^+_p(\boldsymbol{x}) - \boldsymbol{V}^-_q(\boldsymbol{x}).
$$

Read $\boldsymbol{V}^+_p(\boldsymbol{x})$ as the kernel-weighted average of the nearby data, minus $\boldsymbol{x}$: a step from $\boldsymbol{x}$ to the local mean of the data, which is the classical mean-shift step (Cheng, 1995). $\boldsymbol{V}^-_q$ is the same step toward the local mean of the generated samples. The drift attracts each sample toward the data and repels it from the other samples. In practice the normalised weights are a softmax over the samples in a batch, with logits $-\lVert\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{y}\rVert/\tau$.

:::proposition[Combined form, anti-symmetry and equilibrium (Deng et al., 2026)]
With $Z_p = \mathbb{E}_p[k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}^+)]$ and $Z_q = \mathbb{E}_q[k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}^-)]$,
$$
\boldsymbol{V}_{p,q}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \frac{1}{Z_pZ_q}\,\mathbb{E}_{p,q}\big[k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}^+)\,k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}^-)\,(\boldsymbol{y}^+ - \boldsymbol{y}^-)\big].
$$
Consequently $\boldsymbol{V}_{p,q} = -\boldsymbol{V}_{q,p}$, and if $q = p$ then $\boldsymbol{V}_{p,q} = \mathbf{0}$ everywhere.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. Common denominator.** Write $k^\pm = k(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}^\pm)$. Then
$\boldsymbol{V}_{p,q} = \frac{1}{Z_pZ_q}\big(Z_q\,\mathbb{E}_p[k^+(\boldsymbol{y}^+ - \boldsymbol{x})] - Z_p\,\mathbb{E}_q[k^-(\boldsymbol{y}^- - \boldsymbol{x})]\big)$.

**Step 2. One joint expectation.** With $\boldsymbol{y}^+$ and $\boldsymbol{y}^-$ independent, $Z_q\,\mathbb{E}_p[k^+(\boldsymbol{y}^+ - \boldsymbol{x})] = \mathbb{E}_{p,q}[k^+k^-(\boldsymbol{y}^+ - \boldsymbol{x})]$, and likewise for the second term. Their difference is $\mathbb{E}_{p,q}[k^+k^-(\boldsymbol{y}^+ - \boldsymbol{y}^-)]$, because the $\boldsymbol{x}$ terms cancel.

**Step 3. Anti-symmetry.** Swapping $p$ and $q$ swaps the roles of $\boldsymbol{y}^+$ and $\boldsymbol{y}^-$. That leaves $Z_pZ_q$ and $k^+k^-$ unchanged and flips the sign of $\boldsymbol{y}^+ - \boldsymbol{y}^-$.

**Step 4. Equilibrium.** If $q = p$, then $\boldsymbol{V}_{p,p} = -\boldsymbol{V}_{p,p}$, so it is zero.
:::

The converse, that $\boldsymbol{V} = \mathbf{0}$ forces $q = p$, is not true for arbitrary vector fields. The authors give an argument that it holds generically for this construction, under assumptions, rather than a proof. They also show that breaking the anti-symmetry makes training fail.

**The training loss** is a regression of each output onto itself moved by the drift:

$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\,\big\lVert \boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}) - \operatorname{sg}\big[\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}) + \boldsymbol{V}_{p,q_\theta}(\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}))\big] \big\rVert^2 .
$$

:::proposition[What a gradient step does]
The loss value is $\mathbb{E}\lVert\boldsymbol{V}\rVert^2$, and its gradient is $\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L} = -2\,\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\big[(\partial_\theta\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}))^\top\boldsymbol{V}(\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}))\big]$. A small step $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}$ moves each output by $2\eta\,\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}\big[\mathbf{K}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}', \boldsymbol{\varepsilon})\,\boldsymbol{V}(\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}))\big] + O(\eta^2)$, where $\mathbf{K}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}', \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}) = \partial_\theta\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}')\,\partial_\theta\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})^\top$.
:::

:::proof
**Step 1. The value.** Inside the norm, $\boldsymbol{G} - (\boldsymbol{G} + \boldsymbol{V}) = -\boldsymbol{V}$.

**Step 2. The gradient.** The stop-gradient freezes the target, so only the first $\boldsymbol{G}_\theta$ is differentiated: $\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L} = 2\,\mathbb{E}\big[(\partial_\theta\boldsymbol{G}_\theta)^\top(\boldsymbol{G}_\theta - \boldsymbol{G}_\theta - \boldsymbol{V})\big] = -2\,\mathbb{E}\big[(\partial_\theta\boldsymbol{G}_\theta)^\top\boldsymbol{V}\big]$.

**Step 3. The outputs.** To first order, $\boldsymbol{G}_{\theta + \delta\theta}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}') = \boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}') + \partial_\theta\boldsymbol{G}_\theta(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}')\,\delta\theta$. Substitute $\delta\theta = -\eta\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}$.
:::

So training is a particle method whose particles are the network's outputs. Each step moves them a little along the drift, smoothed across outputs by the network's tangent kernel $\mathbf{K}$, and the drift is then recomputed from the new outputs. The stop-gradient matters: $q_\theta$ appears inside $\boldsymbol{V}$, and training does not differentiate through it. It is not gradient descent on $\mathbb{E}\lVert\boldsymbol{V}\rVert^2$, but a fixed-point iteration whose fixed points are the equilibria $\boldsymbol{V} = \mathbf{0}$.

**Relation to MMD.** The authors point out that any discrepancy that is zero when $q = p$, minimised by moving samples, implies a drifting field, the negative gradient of the loss with respect to a sample. For MMD that field is the difference between the average kernel gradient over the data and over the generated samples, which is the particle velocity of an MMD gradient flow (Arbel, Korba, Salim and Gretton, 2019). Drifting uses normalised, mean-shift weights instead, and the authors report that they could not get reasonable results with the MMD formulation in their experiments. Unlike DMD, drifting needs no pretrained score network: only samples of the data and of the generator.

**Guidance.** Classifier-free guidance enters through the negatives. For a class $c$, the negatives are drawn from the mixture $\tilde q = (1 - \gamma)\,q_\theta(\cdot \mid c) + \gamma\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(\cdot \mid \varnothing)$ of generated samples and unconditional data. At equilibrium $\tilde q = p_{\mathrm{data}}(\cdot \mid c)$, so solving for the generator gives $q_\theta(\cdot \mid c) = \alpha\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(\cdot \mid c) - (\alpha - 1)\,p_{\mathrm{data}}(\cdot \mid \varnothing)$ with $\alpha = 1/(1 - \gamma)$. This is the linear extrapolation that guidance performs, now built into a one-step generator. The scale is sampled during training and given to the network as an input, so it can be changed at sampling time.

**At scale.** On images the field is computed in the feature space of a pretrained self-supervised encoder, used only during training. On ImageNet 256×256 the paper reports one-step FID 1.54 in latent space and 1.61 in pixel space, the best one-step results on that benchmark at publication. On robot-control tasks, a one-step drifting policy matches or beats a 100-step diffusion policy on many tasks. Li and Zhu (2026) connect drifting back to the first half of this post. They split a transport into a long flow map and a short final step with a closed-form optimal velocity; as the final step shrinks, this recovers the drifting field plus a correction term.

**On the toy.** The generator is the same small network as the other models, with no time input. The positives are a batch of 1024 data points; the negatives are the batch of 1024 outputs, each excluding itself. The kernel is the published one with a fixed $\tau = 0.5$. There is no encoder, since 2-D points are their own features. The figure shows the field along training. Faint dots are data, solid dots are generated samples, and the arrows show where each sample is told to move, at true scale.

*What to try.* At step 0 the generator puts everything near the centre. The repulsion term spreads the samples out, and the attraction pulls them toward the nearest data. By step 100 the samples reach the ring, and by step 12,800 they sit on the modes, with arrows that have almost vanished. Press "set q = p" to replace the generated samples with fresh data. The field is then the finite-sample residue of anti-symmetry: mean $|\boldsymbol{V}|$ is 0.031, about the size it reaches at the end of training. After 30,000 steps, 92% of one-step samples are on a mode, and the energy distance to the data is within the noise of comparing two data samples.

The table gives the percentage of 4000 samples that land on a mode with 1, 2, 4 and 8 network calls, and the energy distance (ED) to the data after one call ($\times 10^{-3}$). On a mode means within three standard deviations of a centre; the data itself scores 98.8%. Two independent sets of 2000 data points give energy distances between 0.6 and 4.6 over ten draws, so anything in that range is as close as this test can see. Every row covers all eight modes, except the Euler step.

| model (what it learns from) | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | ED |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Euler step, exact velocity | 0 | | | | 1467 |
| exact flow map | 99 | | | | 3.6 |
| distilled map (100,000 exact ODE solves) | 98 | | | | 3.6 |
| consistency distillation (exact teacher) | 89 | 86 | 87 | 89 | 4.0 |
| consistency training (data only) | 68 | 78 | 87 | 90 | 7.5 |
| shortcut model (data only) | 89 | 90 | 95 | 98 | 4.0 |
| MeanFlow, adaptive weight (data only) | 98 | 99.9 | 99.8 | 99.6 | 7.2 |
| MeanFlow, squared error (data only) | 84 | 86 | 95 | 96 | 10.2 |
| drifting model (data only) | 92 | | | | 0.9 |

Four things to read off.

1. **One step works.** Every trained model beats one Euler step of the exact velocity by a wide margin, without straightening any paths. Five of them match or beat the flow-matching post's best one-step result, reflow at 88%.
2. **The teacher is worth about 20 points here.** Consistency distillation and consistency training share the network, the schedule and the budget, and differ only in the target. That gives 89% against 68%: the variance term of Section 4. On images the teacher is a trained model with its own errors, which caps what distillation can reach. That is one reason for DMD2's GAN loss on real data, and for training from scratch.
3. **Models that learn every step size use extra steps best.** The shortcut model goes from 89% to 98% between 1 and 8 calls. Consistency distillation barely moves, because re-noising between jumps throws away part of each jump.
4. **One number is not enough.** MeanFlow with the adaptive weight has the highest share on a mode and one of the worst energy distances, because its modes are too narrow and, with more steps, misplaced (Section 6). The drifting model has 92% on a mode but an energy distance inside the data-against-data range. Its modes are centred and close to the data's width, and its misses are a thin scatter along the ring just outside them.

The toy is two-dimensional, and it says nothing about which method wins on images. There the published comparisons in Sections 4 to 8 are the evidence.

## 10. Which one, when?

- **You have a strong pretrained diffusion or flow model and want 1 to 4 steps for deployment.** Distil it: DMD2 for the best one-step quality (it needs a GAN loss and a second score network); consistency distillation or tuning (sCM, ECT) or Lagrangian flow-map distillation for a simpler recipe.
- **You want to train one model from scratch, with a dial for the number of steps.** MeanFlow and its successors (α-Flow, improved MeanFlow) or shortcut models: they learn every step size, so 1, 2 or 4 steps come from the same weights.
- **You want one step from scratch, and the best published numbers.** Drifting models, at the cost of a feature encoder for training and a batch of negatives per step. On control tasks the authors report one-step policies that match 100-step diffusion policies.
- **You need likelihoods.** None of these. A normalising flow or the ODE of a diffusion model gives them (see the map post).

## Questions

:::question
A network can represent the flow map. Why does flow matching with one Euler step still fail?
:::

:::answer
Flow matching does not train the network to represent the flow map. It trains it to represent the velocity, the tangent to each path. One Euler step follows the tangent at the start for the whole interval, and on the linear path that tangent points at the data mean. The network may be perfect and the step still wrong: the error is the integral in Section 1, which vanishes only for straight paths run at constant speed.
:::

:::question
Consistency training uses no teacher. Where does it learn about the ODE?
:::

:::answer
From the same place flow matching does: each pair's velocity $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{x}_0$, whose conditional mean is the marginal velocity. Section 4 shows that substituting it for a teacher's velocity changes the gradient only at second order in the grid spacing. The price is variance, which is why consistency training needs smaller steps, schedules and more care than distillation.
:::

:::question
MeanFlow's target contains the network itself. What stops it from settling on a wrong answer that agrees with itself?
:::

:::answer
Section 6 shows that the identity, holding for all $r \le t$, determines $\boldsymbol{u}$ uniquely given the velocity. The velocity enters the target directly, through $\boldsymbol{w}$, and directly fixes the diagonal $r = t$, where the loss is flow matching. A wrong $\boldsymbol{u}$ that agrees with itself would violate the identity somewhere. What the stop-gradient changes is the dynamics: training is a fixed-point iteration, like temporal-difference learning, not plain gradient descent, which is why the share of $r = t$ examples and the loss weighting matter.
:::

:::question
Is a consistency model a flow map?
:::

:::answer
It is the slice $r = 0$ of one: $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}, t) = \boldsymbol{X}_{t\to 0}(\boldsymbol{x})$, and with the parametrisation $\boldsymbol{f} = \boldsymbol{x} - t\boldsymbol{F}$, the network $\boldsymbol{F}$ is the average velocity $\boldsymbol{u}(\boldsymbol{x}, 0, t)$. Because it knows only jumps to data, its multistep sampler re-noises between jumps instead of composing shorter jumps. Two-time models (CTM, shortcut models, MeanFlow) can compose.
:::

:::question
The drifting loss always equals $\mathbb{E}\lVert\boldsymbol{V}\rVert^2$. Why not just minimise that directly?
:::

:::answer
Because $\boldsymbol{V}$ depends on the generator twice: through the point where it is evaluated, and through the negatives, which are the generator's own samples. Differentiating through the negatives would ask the generator to change the field rather than follow it, and the authors' loss deliberately blocks that path with the stop-gradient. Section 8 shows what remains: each step moves the outputs along the field, smoothed by the network's tangent kernel, and the field is recomputed. The fixed points are the equilibria, where the anti-symmetry makes $q = p$ one of them.
:::

## The series, in one paragraph

[The map](/aboutme/blog/generative-models-one-map/) put every deep generative model on one page as a choice of divergence and of how to compute it. [Diffusion models](/aboutme/blog/diffusion-models-from-first-principles/) turned generation into denoising, a regression, and showed that sampling is solving an ODE or SDE. [Flow matching](/aboutme/blog/flow-matching/) showed that the same ODE can be learned by regression on straight lines, and that its paths curve. This post learned the ODE's solution instead of its velocity, or skipped the ODE and matched the distribution. The thread through all four is the same: a hard object is replaced by a regression whose conditional mean is the right answer.
